name: FR-4

claims.claim_text: FR4 names a flammability rating rather than a material. What the industry means by it is a particular class of woven fibreglass and epoxy mix, which is why two boards described as FR4 can differ substantially in their electrical properties.
claims.quote_verbatim: is actually the flammability rating. That's what it stands for
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The board is a glass fabric woven in both directions and encased in epoxy. The glass provides the rigidity, the strength, the dimensional stability and the resistance to warping; the epoxy is the glue that holds it together.
claims.quote_verbatim: they combine this glass weave, which gives it its rigidity
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Cheaper board grades use a loose weave with visible gaps between the bundles, producing a checkerboard of glass and bare resin. A controlled-impedance trace running over glass sees a different dielectric constant from one running over a gap, so its impedance depends on where it happens to sit relative to the weave — an effect real enough to measure with a time-domain reflectometer.
claims.quote_verbatim: if your trace, if your controlled impedance trace happens to be above the glass weave
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The dielectric constant quoted for standard laminate is nominal, around 4.3, with a tolerance that reflects what you are paying for. Tight, repeatable dielectric properties are a premium a standard board simply does not include.
claims.quote_verbatim: they say it's, you know, 4.3 dielectric constant, but it's like, it can be 4.3 plus minus
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Phenolic originally described plastics made with phenol resins such as Bakelite, and technically the term covers a whole class of composites including modern board laminate — which is why the same word describes both a cheap single-sided board and, strictly, the material everyone calls something else.
claims.quote_verbatim: phenolic used to mean just uh plastics are made with phenol resins
claims.speaker: Windell Oskay
claims.episode_title: Open Circuits with Eric Schlaepfer and Windell Oskay

claims.claim_text: A signal travels at the speed of light in the laminate rather than in air, slowed by the square root of the dielectric constant. With a dielectric constant near four, that is a factor of two — which converts every trace length into a delay you can calculate.
claims.quote_verbatim: it slows it down with the square root of the dielectric constant
claims.speaker: Eric Bogatin
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric Bogatin - Tilded Thumb Tenets

claims.claim_text: Light covers a foot per nanosecond in air and about six inches per nanosecond in standard laminate — the rule of thumb that a nanosecond is roughly fifteen centimetres of trace, which is enough to do timing arithmetic in your head at a whiteboard.
claims.quote_verbatim: speed of light in air is a foot per nanosecond. You take that into FR4 and it slows it down by a factor of two
claims.speaker: Eric Bogatin
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric Bogatin - Tilded Thumb Tenets

claims.claim_text: Ordinary laminate carries a ten gigahertz radio and it works. What it will not do is deliver an excellent noise figure — below about half a decibel — which is the point at which the design has to move to a higher-performance substrate.
claims.quote_verbatim: can build a 10 gigahertz radio on an FR4 printed circuit board and it will work
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An interview with Tony Long - Millimeter Microwave Magician

claims.claim_text: High-frequency substrates built on PTFE or ceramics offer low loss tangent, different dielectric constants and far better repeatability, and they take the board out of the commodity supply chain: the plating and etching chemistry differs, the softer material moves during processing, and multilayer construction becomes difficult, so most low-cost vendors will not quote them at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: that have very low loss tangent and different dielectric constants than FR4 and also much more repeatable
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An interview with Tony Long - Millimeter Microwave Magician

claims.claim_text: An eight hundred megahertz instrument front end is achievable on standard laminate with disciplined, tight routing. Multiple gigahertz is where controlled-impedance materials become unavoidable, so the board technology rather than the silicon sets the price floor for a cheap fast instrument.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can do that standard FR4, just, you know, just your regular
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Two independent loss mechanisms bound a high-speed channel: conductor size sets the skin-effect loss and the dielectric sets the dielectric loss. Large conductors in an excellent dielectric go remarkably fast and cost accordingly, while small traces on ordinary laminate are what limit how fast and how far a signal can travel.
claims.quote_verbatim: size of the wires determines your skin effect loss. And the material from which you make the dielectric determines the dielectric losses
claims.speaker: Howard Johnson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Howard Johnson - Winsome Waveform Wizardry

claims.claim_text: Think of it as a speed-distance product. A gigabit across ten inches works on any reasonable board material; ten gigabits across the same ten inches forces a conversation about materials; a hundred gigabits is a serious problem, and the eventual escape from it is optical rather than better laminate.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you want to go a gigabit at 10 inches, it's not a problem on any reasonable PC board material
claims.speaker: Howard Johnson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Howard Johnson - Winsome Waveform Wizardry

claims.claim_text: Copper is deliberately roughened where it meets the laminate to develop peel strength, and at very high data rates the loss depends acutely on that roughness — a surface that is too rough can double the loss. Materials made for these speeds use smoother foil and sacrifice adhesion, so the traces almost lift off if handled carelessly.
claims.quote_verbatim: different board manufacturers use different roughnesses of the copper underneath
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A link between two entirely digital chips is an analog channel once it leaves the package: what matters is the frequency and time response of copper on laminate, and equalising for it is filter theory applied to a signal whose contents are irrelevant to the person designing the path.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a return almost to filter theory
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Standard laminate persists because it is too practical to displace: it solves so many problems at once that the alternatives keep failing to arrive, and predictions of a move to optical interconnect have been made for decades without materialising.
claims.quote_verbatim: is too easy. It's just too practical at the moment
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Henry Ott - Forced FCC Filtering

claims.claim_text: Heating a board from below relies on conduction through the laminate, and the laminate is a poor conductor. Where heat genuinely has to move through the board — high-power lighting being the common case — a metal core rather than glass and epoxy is the answer.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to rely on the heat flow through the, through the FR4 laminate
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Shop bots, 450 mm fabs & redFrog - Pick and Place Palillogy

claims.claim_text: Plastic connectors survive reflow because they are surrounded by air rather than in contact with anything that stores heat. Rest one against the laminate, which does retain heat, and it melts — a useful reminder that thermal mass, not just peak temperature, determines what survives a profile.
claims.quote_verbatim: the reason that the board the plastic connectors survive in in uh in reflow ovens is because they're not touching anything that actually retains heat
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Laminate blackening during reflow is evidence that the oven is lying about its temperature rather than that the profile is aggressive: a station set to 220 or 240 degrees was actually delivering considerably more, which is a common failing of cheap thermocouple front ends.
claims.quote_verbatim: despite setting it to like 240, 220, the FR-4 a few times actually blackened
claims.speaker: Mike Grover

claims.claim_text: Using aluminium, ordinary laminate and standard solder is what lets a small satellite burn up completely on re-entry and remain in the upper atmosphere as particles. A denser material such as tungsten would reach the ground, which is why the approval process treats material choice as a safety question.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're just using aluminum and, you know, FR four and, and standard solder, that stuff just burns up
claims.speaker: Brock Lameres

claims.claim_text: Milling standard laminate aerosolises fibreglass — glass shards small enough to breathe and to get into your eyes — which is why desktop milling machines use a softer material and why cutting the real thing demands extraction rather than a workshop vacuum afterwards.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're aerating fiberglass, which is already, like, you know, little tiny shards of glass
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: If laminate is going to be milled, the enclosure and the vacuum extraction are not accessories. The dust is the hazard, and a cheaper open machine can be made acceptable by adding extraction rather than by working carefully.
claims.quote_verbatim: which is going to produce a lot of glass dust, which you don't want to inhale
claims.speaker: Mike Grover

claims.claim_text: Choosing to mill standard laminate rather than the softer prototyping material comes down to what the finished board must be: thicknesses below the usual 1.6 millimetres, ordinary availability from bulk suppliers, better heat resistance and a more robust copper bond — and the prototype then resembles the production board it is meant to predict.
claims.quote_verbatim: want thinner than 1.6
claims.speaker: Mike Grover

claims.claim_text: Laser ablation works on the softer phenolic material and not on glass-epoxy laminate for a specific reason: carbonising the epoxy leaves a residue that conducts, so the process that removes copper cleanly from one substrate leaves conductive tracks across the other.
claims.quote_verbatim: It technically is conductive
claims.speaker: Stephen Hawes
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: A properly made double-sided board costs a few dollars, which leaves in-house board making justified by time rather than money: the only real argument for the machine is needing something within the hour, and anything beyond a one-off is sent out anyway.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can buy a proper FR4 double-sided board for almost, they're practically good for like for five bucks
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Shifting Away From DIY - Pedetentious PnP Progress

claims.claim_text: Boards a tenth of a millimetre thick are available and are not exotic: the material is the same pre-preg stock that multilayer fabs already hold for inner layers, so asking for it is a matter of finding a vendor willing rather than sourcing a special material.
claims.quote_verbatim: found a company that will make 0.1 millimeter FR4 boards
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Where the laminate itself contributes the capacitance limiting a high-impedance divider, the remedy is to remove it: cutting the material away around the divider takes the dielectric out of the circuit rather than trying to compensate for it.
claims.quote_verbatim: finally gave up on trying to control the bad capacitance of a FR4 material
claims.speaker: Dave Taylor
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dave Taylor - Multi-talented Meter Maker

claims.claim_text: A dense phone board is noticeably heavy in the hand because it is mostly copper with very little laminate — the substrate reduced to just enough to separate the layers, since anything more is volume that could have been conductor.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's not much FR4 in these. Yeah. It's mostly copper
claims.speaker: Scotty Allen

claims.claim_text: Scrap board material makes excellent structural fibreglass — high-strength rocket fins in one case — which is worth remembering when the alternative is buying sheet stock: copper-clad or blank, it is a versatile mechanical material in its own right.
claims.quote_verbatim: they turned it into fins for their rocket experiments
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Removing the solder mask over an area lets light pass through the laminate itself, which glows and diffuses — a way to build an illuminated indicator into the board with no additional parts beyond the emitter behind it.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can remove the solder mask and you can have the FR4 actually light up
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Hiding the substrate in a three-dimensional board viewer and looking only at the copper and vias is one of the most effective ways to learn layout, because it forces the mental jump from lines on a screen to a stack of connected conductors.
claims.quote_verbatim: to turn off the FR4 visualization and just look at the vias
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

attribution_notes: attribution_reliable was not trusted. ep476 records Kendall Castor-Perry's account of copper roughness and high-speed channels under Dave Jones's name; the surrounding turns do not disambiguate it cleanly, so it is kept as recorded rather than reassigned.

ep454 (Mike Grover), ep686 (Stephen Hawes), ep609 (Windell Oskay), ep497 (Brock LaMeres) and ep252 (Eric Bogatin) label host questions with the guest's name; only material unambiguously the guest's own was used.
One passage carries episode: null — a discussion of thin laminate used as a structural baseplate in a quadcopter kit — and was dropped as uncitable.
Passing remarks about board colour, aesthetics and pricing of milling machines were excluded as non-transferable.
